title: A Queen's Victory Temple
text: At Pattadakal in Karnataka, Chalukya builders of the 7th and 8th centuries blended temple styles from northern and southern India. Nine Hindu temples and a Jain sanctuary stand together here. The masterpiece is the Temple of Virupaksha, built around 740 by Queen Lokamahadevi to celebrate her husband's victory over the kings from the South.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Group of Monuments at Pattadakal

title: The Great Monastery of Paharpur
text: A clay seal names King Dharmapala, who ruled from 770 to 810, as the first builder of Somapura Mahavihara, the Great Monastery in north-west Bangladesh. Its central shrine rose about 70 feet, wrapped in bands of terracotta plaques, and in its final phase 177 cells formed its outer wall. It stayed a famous centre of learning until the 12th century and influenced Buddhist buildings as far away as Cambodia.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Ruins of the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur

title: A Brick City Swallowed by Jungle
text: In the 15th century the general Ulugh Khan Jahan built the city of Khalifatabad, now Bagerhat, in south-west Bangladesh within a few years. Its baked-brick mosques, tombs, bridges, roads and water tanks show expert planning, and it needed no walls because people could retreat into the Sundarbans mangroves. After Khan Jahan died in 1459, the jungle covered the city.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat

title: A Temple Topped With Floating Bricks
text: Work on the Rudreshwara, or Ramappa, Temple in Telangana began in 1213 and is thought to have gone on for some 40 years. Kakatiya builders gave its tower lightweight porous "floating bricks" to make the roof less heavy. Its bracket figures, carved from hard dolerite with a metal-like shine, show dancers in the regional styles of Kakatiya culture.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple, Telangana

title: An Upside-Down Temple for Water
text: Rani-ki-Vav, the Queen's Stepwell at Patan in Gujarat, was first built as a memorial to a king in the 11th century. Designed as an upside-down temple honouring the sacredness of water, it steps down seven levels past more than 500 main sculptures. At its deepest level a tank lies 23 metres below ground, and the well shaft goes down 30 metres.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Rani-ki-Vav (the Queen's Stepwell) at Patan, Gujarat

title: Sculptors Who Signed Their Work
text: In the 12th and 13th centuries, Hoysala architects in Karnataka invented a new temple style to give their kingdom its own identity. Star-shaped shrines at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura are covered in lifelike carvings, including the legend of Sala killing a tiger. Unusually for the subcontinent, the artists left many signatures, a sign of the high standing they enjoyed.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas

title: Kalhana's River of Kings
text: In 1148 the Kashmiri poet Kalhana wrote the Rajatarangini, a history of Kashmir in 7,826 Sanskrit verses split into eight books. He studied inscriptions about temples and land grants, coins, ruins and family records. His ideal was a poet who, like a judge, records the past free from love or hatred, though his early chapters still mix legend with history.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Rajatarangini

title: A Bengali Teacher Heads for Tibet
text: Atish Dipankar was born in Vajrayogini village in Vikramapura, Bengal, and became head of the great Vikramashila monastery. Invited by a Buddhist king of Tibet, he began his journey there in 1040. In Tibet he wrote, translated and edited more than two hundred books, many from Sanskrit into Tibetan. He died near Lhasa, and in 1978 his ashes were brought to Dhaka.

source.name: Banglapedia: Dipankar Srijnan, Atish

title: A Young Newar Artist Goes East
text: The Newars are the traditional people of Nepal's Kathmandu Valley. In 1261 Pakpa invited a young Newar artist, Anige (also called Araniko), to the Yuan court of the Mongol rulers, along with 24 other Himalayan artisans. Between 1270 and 1279 Anige helped design and oversee the White Stupa in Beijing, and he rose to become director of all artisan classes.

source.name: Rubin Museum, Project Himalayan Art (Isabelle Charleux): Newar Artist's Buddhist Monument for the Mongol Rulers in Beijing

title: Underground Homes in Kashmir
place: Burzahom, Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, India
text: From about 3000 BCE, the first settlers at Burzahom in Kashmir lived in pits dug into the soil with long stone axes, and their cut-marks can still be seen. Some pits were 3.95 metres deep, wide at the bottom and likely roofed with birch. People made tools of stone, bone and antler, and an engraved stone shows a hunting scene with a human and a dog.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative Lists: The Neolithic Settlement of Burzahom

title: A Town Planned From Day One
place: Rehman Dheri, near Dera Ismail Khan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
text: Around 3300 BCE people began a settlement at Rehman Dheri in north-west Pakistan, and it seems to have had a formal plan from its earliest phases. A wall enclosed a grid of streets and lanes dividing regular blocks. Walls of houses still show up in the morning dew, and kilns and slag mark small workshops. It is a rare, undisturbed picture of how towns began in South Asia.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative Lists: Archaeological Site of Rehman Dheri

title: Letters on Pots at Keeladi
text: According to Tamil Nadu's Department of Archaeology, carbon dating puts some finds at Keeladi as early as 580 BCE. Its people built brick walls and clay floors, left bones of cows, buffalo and goats that hint at farming, and played board games. They wrote on pottery in the Tamil-Brahmi script, and digs have turned up spinning and weaving tools, cloth-dyeing works, brick kilns and pottery workshops.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine (Livia Gershon): Archaeologists Unearth Ancient Dagger Linked to Enigmatic Indian Civilization

title: The Oldest Known Case of Leprosy
text: At Balathal in Rajasthan, a middle-aged man was buried inside a stone enclosure, in layers of burned cow dung ash. Changes to the bones of his nose and upper jaw point to leprosy, showing the disease was present in India by about 2000 BCE. It is the oldest documented skeletal evidence for the disease, and the authors say the unusual burial may reflect how people with leprosy were treated.

source.name: PLOS ONE (Robbins et al.): Ancient Skeletal Evidence for Leprosy in India (2000 B.C.)

title: Seventy Who Walked Out of Kalunga
text: In 1814 the East India Company went to war with Gorkha. At the hill fort of Kalunga, also called Nalapani, about 600 Goorkha soldiers under Balbhadra held off attackers, and the British commander Gillespie was killed on 31 October. On the night of 29 November the 70 survivors charged out and escaped. Two memorials were later raised, one to each side.

source.name: The Gurkha Museum: The Battle of Kalunga

title: Newspapers Under Police Watch
text: On March 14, 1878, during Viceroy Lord Lytton's rule, the Vernacular Press Act became law. Papers had to hand police the proof sheets of their contents before printing, and police rather than judges decided what was seditious. Papers such as Somprakash, Amrita Bazar Patrika and Dacca Prakash were targeted. Many papers were fined and editors jailed until Lord Ripon's government withdrew the Act.

source.name: Banglapedia (Sirajul Islam): Vernacular Press Act, 1878

title: Half a Million Tombs on Makli Hill
text: Near the Indus delta in Sindh, the hill of Makli holds about half a million tombs and graves, one of the largest cemeteries in the world. Kings, queens, saints and scholars of nearby Thatta lie here. Among the finest stone tombs is that of Jam Nizamuddin II, who reigned from 1461 to 1509. The monuments fuse Gujarat-style Hindu and Mughal influences into a local style.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historical Monuments at Makli, Thatta

title: One Woman's DNA From Rakhigarhi
text: Rakhigarhi in Haryana was the largest town of the Indus Valley Civilisation, and charcoal from its main living area dates to 2800–2300 BCE. Scientists screened 61 skeletons from its graves before finding a tiny amount of DNA in one woman's remains. Her genes point to ancestors related to ancient Iranians and South-east Asian hunter-gatherers, though those ancestors almost certainly lived in South Asia for thousands of years.

source.name: Cell, via PubMed Central (Shinde et al.): An Ancient Harappan Genome Lacks Ancestry from Steppe Pastoralists or Iranian Farmers

source2.name: Nature India (Biplab Das): Where did the Indus Valley people come from?

title: A Capital Left to the Jungle
place: Anuradhapura, North Central Province, Sri Lanka
text: Anuradhapura grew around a cutting of the Buddha's fig tree, brought in the 3rd century BCE by Sanghamitta, founder of an order of Buddhist nuns. It flourished as Sri Lanka's political and religious capital for 1,300 years, until an invasion in 993 led to its abandonment. Polonnaruwa became the new capital, and Anuradhapura's palaces and monasteries lay hidden in dense jungle for many years.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Sacred City of Anuradhapura

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Ancient City of Polonnaruwa

title: A River Becomes a Border
text: Ranjit Singh, Maharaja of the Punjab, hoped to bring together all the Sikh lands up to the vicinity of Delhi, but the English thwarted him. In 1809 they made him sign the Treaty of Amritsar, which fixed the Sutlej River as his eastern boundary. He turned his ambitions elsewhere, and by 1820 he ruled the whole Punjab between the Sutlej and Indus rivers.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Khushwant Singh): Ranjit Singh

title: Bhutan Chooses a King
text: For centuries Bhutan had two supreme authorities: a dharma raja for spiritual affairs and a deb raja for worldly matters, while regional governors often fought their way into office. In 1907, after the dharma raja died and the deb raja withdrew into a life of contemplation, a council of lamas, abbots, councillors and laymen chose Ugyen Wangchuk of Tongsa as hereditary king.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Pradyumna P. Karan): Bhutan, History

title: Mehrgarh Packs Up and Moves
text: Near the Bolan Pass in Balochistan, people lived at Mehrgarh for thousands of years, leaving layers over 11 metres deep from the seventh to the third millennium BCE. Small mud-brick storerooms and early cattle and barley farming grew into a Bronze Age village with its own crafts. By 2600 BCE the settlement had shifted to Naushero, some six kilometres south.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative Lists: Archaeological Site of Mehrgarh

title: The Great Kathmandu Earthquake
text: A chronicle from Kathmandu records that on June 7, 1255, an earthquake brought down temples and houses, killing one third of the inhabitants, including King Abhaya Malladeva. Survivors left the country, and aftershocks were felt for four months. Geologists have since traced its surface rupture east of the city, on a similar stretch of fault to the rupture of the great 1934 earthquake.

source.name: Earth, Planets and Space (Bollinger et al.): Slip deficit in central Nepal: omen for a repeat of the 1344 AD earthquake?
